source.title: Mixture of Experts Made Intrinsically Interpretable
source.authors: Xing-Yi Yang; Constantin Venhoff; Ashkan Khakzar; Christian Schroeder de Witt; P. Dokania; A. Bibi; P. Torr

page_placements.theme: Architecture, width, sparsity and training change counts of concept-aligned units or superposition proxies

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendix are present. There are minor text-extraction/typographical errors, but no material cutoff or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether architectural choices and activation sparsity affect neuron interpretability, using chess board-state alignment and reconstruction measures rather than the original sources’ neuron visualizations.
record.gate_note: The study does not directly count neurons that respond to unrelated concepts. Its chess board-state coverage and reconstruction scores are proxy measures of interpretability. The natural-language auto-interpretability experiment measures how well an explainer’s descriptions predict activation; it does not report a rate of polysemantic neurons. The paper explicitly compares architectural and activation-function choices, and varies width and sparsity.
record.test_reason: The paper takes polysemanticity and superposition as its motivating premise and proposes an architecture (MoE-X). It never counts or rates polysemantic neurons. All its chess results use BSP coverage and reconstruction: whether some neuron or feature aligns with each board-state property. These are aggregate interpretability proxies, not a share of neurons responding to unrelated inputs. Table 1 and Table 3 mainly compare the authors' own method with baselines and ablations. The natural-language detection score measures explanation quality, not polysemantic prevalence. Superposition is stated only as a hypothesis ('We hypothize'), not tested. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that width and sparsity are key to interpretability and present MoE-X as matching dense-model performance while being more interpretable. On chess, MoE-X has the best reconstruction score. In natural language, MoE-X Small matches and MoE-X Medium surpasses GPT-2+SAE on detection score. They also argue prior designs (SoLU, Monet) lack empirical support. Their claim that MoE-X reduces polysemanticity is asserted, not directly measured.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses chess board-state coverage/reconstruction, architecture comparisons, and an automated explanation-detection pipeline rather than the original sources’ methods for identifying and interpreting individual polysemantic neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability varies with MLP width, activation sparsity, activation function, routing design, model size, and layer. The paper reports that extreme sparsity is not always best and that the chess reconstruction score peaks at layer 6.

fits_no_version.finding: In 8-layer chess GPT-2-like models, wider MLPs (higher α or d) and sparser activations (ReLU, Top-k) raise BSP coverage. Gains are larger in bigger models, and the most extreme sparsity is not always best.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider and sparser MLP hidden layers improve alignment of neurons with ground-truth board-state features.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched active parameters on chess, SoLU, GEGLU, ReLU, Monet and PEER score below GELU on coverage and reconstruction. Switch and MoE-X score above it (MoE-X reconstruction 0.840 vs 0.608), with similar validation loss (0.211 vs 0.213).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectures marketed as more monosemantic (SoLU, Monet) do not improve board-state alignment proxies, while sparse MoE layers do, without loss in task performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablation: sparsity-aware routing raises reconstruction from 0.734 to 0.829. ReLU experts alone lower coverage (0.404) but raise reconstruction slightly. Both together give 0.428 coverage and 0.840 reconstruction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparsity-aware routing in MoE improves board-state reconstruction proxies.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), as stated in the study metadata
record.problems: The study does not directly measure polysemantic-neuron prevalence or establish the proposed superposition mechanism. Its principal chess interpretability measures are proxies based on board-state alignment/reconstruction. Numerical uncertainty is not reported for the chess table results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant numeric chess coverage or reconstruction results were left out. Natural-language auto-interpretability detection accuracy and its activation-quantile plot were not entered as rows because they evaluate explanation detection rather than the prevalence of polysemantic neurons.

untested.parts: No share of LM MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens is reported. Auto-interp detection scores cover 1,000 random features, not polysemantic prevalence.
Superposition is asserted as a hypothesis only. Feature count vs neuron capacity is never measured.
No share of polysemantic neurons is measured across activation functions or architectures. Only board-state alignment proxies are reported.
Not tested. The study only notes that its scores vary by layer (peak at layer 6) and by sparsity level.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V3 and V5 labels were dropped. No row measures a polysemantic-neuron share or tests superposition. Coverage and reconstruction score whether some unit aligns with each board property, which is a different construct. The SoLU result (lower than GELU on these proxies) is a useful contrast with the SoLU original but does not test its polysemantic-share claim. The following are not in the rows but are also proxy results that would belong under fits_no_version, not versions: Table 4 (upcycling vs scratch), Fig 11 (layer dependence), Appendix C (L0 313 to 166 with sparsity routing) and Fig 8 (detection accuracy).

versions.untested_parts: No vision classifier or InceptionV1 neurons are examined.
The paper does not measure the share of language-model MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.

The paper proposes superposition as an explanation and varies width/sparsity, but does not directly measure the number of represented features relative to neuron capacity or establish that capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
No test isolates initialization, regularization, or training noise as a source of polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.

Polysemantic-neuron share is not directly counted. The study tests selected activation functions and MoE architectures, primarily with chess interpretability metrics; it does not test modern convnets or a broad range of regularization methods.
The study does not revisit canonical mixed neurons to determine whether their inputs share a feature or job.
The auto-interpretability experiment samples activation quantiles, but does not test whether classifying neurons as polysemantic changes with the activation range or explanation-scoring method.
